query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A single tailored surface treatment (via laser or plasma processing) that pre-engineers a reactive interface on the CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy will promote the in situ formation of a stable oxide nanocomposite layer during sliding. This self-adaptive surface layer will maintain low friction and wear rates consistently over a broad temperature range (room temperature to 800 °C) under variable load and oxidizing conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy in its as-fabricated state without any pre-engineered surface modification, which exhibits temperature-dependent friction and wear behavior.
generation.intervention: Application of a controlled laser or plasma surface treatment to create a precursor surface structure that favours the formation and stabilization of an oxide nanocomposite layer during sliding.
generation.conditions: Sliding tribotesting conducted from room temperature up to 800 °C, under both low and high normal loads in an oxidizing (ambient) environment, thereby spanning the full operational regime.
generation.structural_mediator: A reactive oxide nanocomposite surface layer that forms or is activated in situ during sliding.
generation.mechanism: The engineered surface modification creates a reactive interface that, upon exposure to frictional heat and oxygen during sliding, rapidly transforms into a lubricious, self-healing oxide layer. This layer minimizes adhesive wear and accommodates high shear stresses, thereby lowering the friction coefficient and wear rate compared to the untreated alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated CoCrFeNi alloy, the surface-treated alloy will demonstrate a consistently lower friction coefficient and wear rate across the full temperature range (room temperature to 800 °C) and under varied load conditions.
generation.baseline: The untreated CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy, which tends to form only transient or non-robust oxide layers that do not sufficiently control friction and wear over wide temperature ranges.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the intervention is assumed to hold under oxidizing conditions and within the tested load ranges. Under extremely high loads, prolonged sliding, or in non-oxidizing environments, the formation and stability of the oxide layer may be compromised.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the long-term durability of the engineered surface layer under extended operating conditions and potential sensitivity to deviations in environmental oxygen levels or unexpected thermal stresses during sliding.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNi alloy samples: one group receives the tailored laser or plasma surface treatment, while the control group remains untreated. Subject both groups to sliding tribotesting over a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C at various normal loads (both low and high) in an ambient oxidizing environment.
measurements: Coefficient of friction versus temperature and load
Wear rate (volume loss) measured via interferometry or profilometry
Surface characterization (SEM/EDS) to confirm the formation and stability of the oxide nanocomposite layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the surface-treated samples do not consistently exhibit statistically significant (e.g., ≥20% lower) friction coefficients and wear rates across the entire tested temperature and load range compared to the untreated baseline, or if the engineered oxide layer degrades or fails to form under the specified conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Our work uncovers a practical avenue for tailoring wear properties with multicomponent heterostructures over a wide temperature range.

The SEM images and EDS scans presented in Figs. 1 and 2 strongly suggest that adhesive forces acting between the HEA and the sapphire spheres led to material transfer from CoCrFeMnNi to the counter body. The worn surface of CoCrFeMnNi after 0.5 and one cycle in Fig. 1a and b shows flake-like delamination within the wear track. We speculate that material was pulled out of the surface due to strong adhesive forces. The oval-shaped region in the wear track after one cycle (Fig. 1b, upper white arrow) is most likely re-deposited CoCrFeMnNi that had been transferred to the sapphire sphere and then back to the wear track. Similar behavior for a dry contact of CoCrFeMnNi in contact with a Si3N4 sphere was reported in the literature [], albeit for fretting conditions. An adhesive wear mechanism was also observed for other compositional complex alloys []. This being said and while there seems to be growing evidence for higher adhesive forces with HEAs, a statement about the universality of this behavior will require more and detailed studies. Material transfer changes the friction contact to a self-mated contact.

Since their discovery in 2004,, high entropy alloys (HEAs) have been extensively investigated and shown to exhibit remarkable thermomechanical properties,. Studies of grain-size dependent mechanical behavior are limited,, however, especially in the regime of ultra-nanocrystalline grain size where softening (i.e. inverse Hall-Petch behavior) occurs. Recent work has also shown that these alloys are ideally suited for processing using laser-based additive manufacturing techniques, as they exhibit high phase stability and derive much of their strength from thermal history-insensitive mechanisms like solution strengthening. While recent publications have presented experimental evidence of low friction or high wear resistance (but typically not both) with HEAs, they were performed in environments where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide surface films was prevalent. Wear-related energy and material loss cost over 2500 Billion Euro per year. Traditional wisdom suggests that high-strength materials reveal low wear rates, yet, their plastic deformation mechanisms also influence their wear performance. High strength and homogeneous deformation behavior, which allow accommodating plastic strain without cracking or localized brittle fracture, are crucial for developing wear-resistant metals. Here, we present an approach to achieve superior wear resistance via in-situ formation of a strong and deformable oxide nanocomposite surface during wear, by reaction of the metal surface with its oxidative environment, a principle that we refer to as ‘reactive wear protection’. We design a TiNbZr-Ag alloy that forms an amorphous-crystalline oxidic nanocomposite surface layer upon dry sliding. The strong (2.4 GPa yield strength) and deformable (homogeneous deformation to 20% strain) nanocomposite surface reduces the wear rate of the TiNbZr-Ag alloy by an order of magnitude. In the present study, the tribological properties of different grain sizes CoCrFeMnNi HEAs were systematically analyzed based on sliding experiments and worn surface morphology characterization under different sliding speeds and normal loads. The results can be summarized as follows: Under the normal low load and low sliding speed, the main wear mechanism of FG and CG samples is adhesive wear. With the increase in sliding speed, the wear mechanisms are adhesive wear and oxidation wear. However, the material of CG is easy to soften under the action of friction heat during high sliding speed, and the oxide layer formed is easy to fracture. Under the normal high load, the wear mechanisms of FG and CG samples are mainly adhesive wear, oxidation wear, and plastic deformation with the increase of sliding speed. The oxidation layer formed on CG sample has many cracks, and the wear surface of CG sample also has plastic deformation, resulting in an increase in friction coefficient and specific wear rate and a decrease in wear resistance. Therefore, under high load and low load, FG sample has good wear resistance due to its high surface strength.

decision.trend: Early studies first aimed at improving high‐entropy alloy performance by modifying their bulk microstructure and composition – for example, adding oxide nanoparticle reinforcements and alloying elements – to enhance mechanical strength and high‐temperature stability. More recently, work on related self‐lubricating systems has shifted toward engineering adaptive surface layers (or reactive nanocomposite interfaces) that develop in situ during sliding. These studies have demonstrated that when the surface reacts appropriately with the environment, a lubricious layer forms that lowers friction and wear at elevated temperatures. However, while these interventions have shown promise in similar systems or modified alloy compositions, the baseline CoCrFeNi matrix has yet to be endowed with a self-adaptive, temperature-robust interface.
decision.unsolved: The remaining challenge is to devise a single, controllable intervention that triggers formation or stabilization of a dynamic, self-healing tribolayer on the CoCrFeNi surface. This layer must reliably sustain low friction and wear over a very wide range of temperatures, loads, and environments, without resorting to altering the alloy’s bulk composition.
decision.lever: Implement a tailored surface treatment (e.g., via laser or plasma processing) designed to pre-engineer or promote in situ formation of a reactive oxide nanocomposite layer during sliding.
decision.why: This approach aligns with the observed trend in tribological research – from bulk modifications to adaptive interfacial design – and directly addresses the challenge by aiming to create a self-lubricating, adaptive surface that forms under operational stresses and temperatures. It circumvents the need for composition changes and targets the mechanism indicated by prior evidence in related systems, while enabling falsifiability through a controlled sliding experiment that tracks the presence and performance of the engineered layer.
